issues.legal_issue: Statutory pre-emption rights granted to specified relatives on the basis of consanguinity violate constitutional equality guarantees when the classification is internally inconsistent and its social justifications are no longer relevant.
material_facts: The challenged provisions gave specified relatives a right to pre-empt sales of agricultural land and village immovable property.
The listed relatives included some relatives of a degree while excluding others, including exclusions based on sex or relationship through women, and the list contained internal inconsistencies.
The relatives had no present ownership right in the property sold, which was fully owned by the vendor.

The Court found that changes in rural life, industrialisation, mechanisation of agriculture, and population movement had weakened the traditional family and village ties relied on to justify the classification.
issues.conclusion: The kinship-based categories in the specified clauses of section 15(1)(a), (b), and (c), and all of section 15(2), were declared unconstitutional for want of reasonable classification and for infringing Articles 14 and 15.
issues.legal_principle: A statutory classification must be reasonable and consistent with the Constitution, considered in light of the Preamble and the Directive Principles in Part IV, including Article 39(c). A classification that is out of tune with the Constitution is unreasonable. The Court assessed the challenged kinship classification principally under Article 14, with Articles 14 and 15 as the constitutional guarantees at issue. It treated the earlier decision in Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, as having upheld a related pre-emption provision on social grounds that were no longer persuasive in the circumstances considered here. Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 724, and Sant Ram v. Labh Singh, A.I.R. 1965 S.C. 314, were also considered in explaining the constitutional treatment of pre-emption rights.

rule.if: constitutional_validity_challenge and kinship_based_preemption and kinship_categories_are_inconsistent and traditional_social_justifications_are_no_longer_relevant

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption scheme in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.kinship_based_preemption: The challenged scheme granted a pre-emption right to specified relatives because of their relationship to the seller.
predicates.kinship_categories_are_inconsistent: The statutory list included some relatives while excluding others of comparable degree or relationship, producing internal inconsistencies.
predicates.traditional_social_justifications_are_no: The social conditions relied on to justify preserving family or village ties had materially weakened, and the relatives had no present ownership right in the property sold.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns a kinship-based pre-emption right and the listed relatives are inconsistently classified while the relied-on social justifications have become irrelevant, the classification is unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Pre-emption rights granted to co-owners are constitutionally valid because co-owners form a distinct class and an outsider's entry may impair common management.
material_facts: The statutory scheme gave other co-owners a pre-emption right in the case of a sale of a share out of jointly owned land or property.
The Court relied on the difficulty of common management when an outsider becomes a co-owner and the benefits of keeping jointly owned property within the existing group of co-owners.
issues.conclusion: The co-owner pre-emption category in the relevant clause of section 15(1)(b) was valid and did not infringe Articles 14 or 15.
issues.legal_principle: A classification of co-owners as a distinct class for pre-emption is reasonable where it protects the practical management and benefits of common ownership. The Court applied Articles 14 and 15 and followed the reasoning in Bhau Ram v. B. Baijnath Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 724, which upheld pre-emption in favour of co-sharers as a reasonable restriction in the public interest. It also referred to Ram Sarup v. Munshi, [1963] 3 S.C.R. 858, in discussing the distinction between kinship-based and co-owner-based pre-emption.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption scheme in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.preemption_benefits_existing_co_owners: The statutory right to pre-empt a sale of a jointly owned share was granted to the other co-owners.
predicates.outsider_entry_may_impair_common_managem: The entry of a new outsider as a co-owner could make common management difficult or diminish the benefits of common ownership.

issues.definition: If a constitutional challenge concerns a pre-emption right for existing co-owners and an outsider's entry may impair common management, the co-owner classification is constitutional.

issues.legal_issue: Pre-emption rights granted to tenants are constitutionally valid because tenants form a distinct class and the right protects their ability to obtain ownership of the land they cultivate.
material_facts: The statutory scheme granted pre-emption rights to tenants holding the land or property sold, or part of it, under a tenancy from the vendor.
The Court considered the protective purpose of enabling a tenant who tills the soil to obtain proprietary rights and avoid losing possession and livelihood to a superior proprietor.
issues.conclusion: The tenant pre-emption categories in the relevant clauses of section 15(1)(a), (b), and (c) were valid and did not infringe Articles 14 or 15.
issues.legal_principle: Tenants may be treated as a distinct class for pre-emption where the right advances land-reform objectives by protecting the tiller of the soil from losing possession and livelihood and by enabling the tenant to obtain proprietary rights. The Court applied Articles 14 and 15 and held the tenant categories reasonable and in the public interest.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A party challenged the constitutionality of a statutory pre-emption scheme in a constitutional proceeding.
predicates.preemption_benefits_a_tenant: The statutory pre-emption right was granted to a tenant holding the property sold, or part of it, under a tenancy from the seller.
predicates.tenant_protection_advances_land_reform: The right protects the tenant's possession and livelihood and advances the objective of enabling the person who cultivates the land to obtain ownership rights.

issues.definition: If a constitutional challenge concerns a pre-emption right for a tenant and the right protects the tenant in a way that advances land-reform objectives, the tenant classification is constitutional.
